source.title: What Converges in the Platonic Representation Hypothesis? Structure over Geometry
source.authors: Junwon You; Mih-Yun Jang; Sang-Woo Mo; Jae-Hun Jung

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present. No apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly evaluates representational alignment across model capacity and argues that convergence depends on whether relational structure or metric geometry is compared. It refines the claim rather than testing the original measures exactly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for relational alignment at local and global scales, distance- and cosine-aware alignment, alternative distance normalization, a Riemannian metric approximation, and video-text representations. Cited findings from prior studies are not recorded as rows. Capacity-trajectory figures are summarized by the paper's reported within-family Spearman statistics; individual model-pair results are not separately tabulated in the text.
record.test_reason: The study measures alignment and its association with model size, separating shared relational structure from quantitative geometry. Its results support structural convergence while qualifying convergence under stricter metric agreement.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that calibrated relational convergence extends to global spanning structure, while stricter quantitative agreement weakens alignment and capacity trends. They reproduce the distinction with cosine agreement, one Riemannian approximation, and video-text data, while limiting their global claim to H0 spanning structure.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a controlled framework of mKNN and H0 skeleton overlap plus distance-aware variants, rather than reproducing the original PRH measurements. It applies aggregation-aware permutation calibration and examines relational structure separately from metric geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment and capacity associations change with distance-agreement stringency τ. The strict regime also separates local and global significance rates. The main weakening pattern is qualitatively robust to alternative distance-normalization quantiles, cosine-similarity agreement, a Riemannian approximation, and video-text inputs.
record.problems: The study uses 1,024 samples per setting and reports aggregate results over model pairs; the full model-pair outcomes are mainly shown in figures. Model size is used as the capacity axis, without a separate task-performance check. The tested representations and data settings are limited, and the Riemannian analysis uses one approximation. The authors note limitations to H0 spanning structure and a fixed-relation formulation of metric agreement.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row cap. Individual model-pair and family-specific figure trajectories are not separately extracted where the paper provides aggregate statistics instead.

untested.parts: Independent capability measurements, arbitrary architectures and training regimes, and extrapolation beyond the sampled size ranges. Vision models are transformers; size is the capacity proxy.
Whether alignment increases with independently established improvements in both modalities' task performance.
Same-architecture comparisons across random initializations and shared features or subspaces across seeds.
Mappings, stitching, interchangeability, and transfer loss.
Out-of-distribution evaluation, controlled input-distribution effects, and sensitivity to the main mKNN neighborhood count. Alternative datasets also change the model setting.
An asymptotic plateau and causal explanations involving shared training data or objectives versus a common representation of reality.

missing.what: Normalization robustness and residual setting dependence: alternative quantiles produce nearly unchanged decay curves, but at τ = 10−4 significant global pairs range from 58 to 109 and local pairs from 176 to 182.

Intermediate capacity associations at τ = 10−1, 10−2 and 10−3. Language-local values are 0.376, 0.269, 0.351; language-global 0.388, 0.353, 0.319; vision-local 0.707, 0.623, 0.478; vision-global 0.722, 0.590, 0.414. These show that weakening is not uniformly monotonic.

record.verdict_notes: All supplied numerical row values match the text. Relative support baselines are normalized means, not perfect agreement. Absolute score decay is partly imposed by the weighting formula; the rank-association tests provide the stronger evidence. Sweep p/q values test τ = 1 against τ = 10−4 and the full distance-aware sweep, excluding Support. States shared across versions are qualified in each row's problem field. Figure-only capacity trajectories are explicitly declared left out, so they are not listed as missing; video-text support significance alone cannot substantiate a scaling verdict. Robustness across alternative metrics does not warrant a limits_scope label against V6.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests capacity-dependent alignment for its vision-language and video-text model pairs, but does not test the full breadth of the claim across arbitrary architectures, objectives, data, or modalities, nor does it measure general model capability separately from nominal model size.
Tests paired image-text and video-text representations across model-size axes, but does not establish that both modalities' independently measured task performance improves in parallel.
No comparison of different random seeds for the same architecture or analysis of shared features or subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
No recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits are tested.

Tests agreement stringency, local versus global supports, cosine versus distance agreement, normalization quantiles, and one Riemannian approximation. Does not test out-of-distribution inputs; it uses the WIT image-text subset and the stated video-text sample.

Tests weakening of capacity association and alignment under stricter metric agreement. It does not test whether shared training data or objectives, rather than a common model of reality, cause the observed alignment.
